_meta.purpose: Starter dataset for rawtocookedcalculator.com. Cooking yield % = cooked weight as a percentage of raw weight. Macros are per 100g RAW food, sourced/cross-referenced from USDA FoodData Central and USDA Table of Cooking Yields for Meat and Poultry, Release 2.
_meta.yield_sources: Yield figures come from five cited authorities: the modern USDA Table of Cooking Yields for Meat and Poultry (2012/2014), USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 102 (1975), USDA FoodData Central raw-vs-cooked nutrient ratios, IFCT 2017 — India's official Indian Food Composition Tables — for soy chunks only, which USDA does not track, and the FAO/Bognar weight-yield tables for the scrambled-egg figure only, which USDA lists only as a recipe made with added milk and fat.
_meta.verification_needed: Spot-check every entry against live USDA FoodData Central (fdc.nal.usda.gov) before publishing, especially chicken (flagship page). Macros for entries added after the initial dataset (veal cutlet, veal roast, spaghetti, chicken drumstick, chicken wings, egg) still need the same spot-check; their yield figures are cited but their macros are standard FoodData Central raw values, not part of the cited yield sources.

meat_poultry_seafood.name: Chicken Wings (whole, with skin)
meat_poultry_seafood.note: Added after the initial dataset. Whole wing, meat and skin, bone in — unlike the other chicken cuts here, which are skinless and boneless. The 74% roasted figure is the whole-wing cooking yield from the USDA Table of Cooking Yields for Meat and Poultry; the simmered-or-stewed (86%) and flour-dredged deep-fried (66%) figures are the other whole-wing preparations that table documents. Macros are standard USDA FoodData Central raw values for chicken wing meat and skin (NDB 05027) and still need the spot-check described in _meta.verification_needed.

meat_poultry_seafood.name: Veal Cutlet
meat_poultry_seafood.note: Macros are standard USDA FoodData Central values for raw veal leg (top round) and still need the spot-check described in _meta.verification_needed.

meat_poultry_seafood.name: Veal Roast (boneless)
meat_poultry_seafood.note: 71% is the all-temperatures average; the sub-options are doneness levels, not cooking methods. Macros are standard USDA FoodData Central values for raw veal (composite of trimmed retail cuts) and still need the spot-check described in _meta.verification_needed.

meat_poultry_seafood.name: Egg (whole, raw, out of shell)
meat_poultry_seafood.note: Added after the initial dataset. Weigh eggs cracked out of the shell. A hard-boiled or poached egg loses essentially no weight — USDA FoodData Central carries the same protein per 100g for raw whole egg and for its boiled and poached entries. Frying and scrambling drive off some water: the 92% pan-fried figure is the raw-vs-cooked protein ratio for USDA's fried-egg entry (NDB 01130), and the 91% scrambled figure is from the FAO/Bognar weight-yield tables, since USDA lists scrambled egg only as a recipe made with added milk and fat. Macros are standard USDA FoodData Central raw whole-egg values (NDB 01123) and still need the spot-check described in _meta.verification_needed.
meat_poultry_seafood.source: USDA FoodData Central (raw vs. cooked entries)

grains_pasta_legumes.name: White Rice (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Grains EXPAND rather than shrink - yield_percent > 100 here means the weight roughly triples. Boiled figure corrected from 300 to 308 in the data-correction pass, matching USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 102.

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Pasta (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Generic dry pasta. Real yields vary meaningfully by shape - this figure sits close to Rigatoni's measured 219%; see the separate spaghetti entry for long pasta.
grains_pasta_legumes.source: USDA FoodData Central (raw vs. cooked entries)

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Spaghetti (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Representative of the measured 265-312% range, which depends on doneness (al dente vs. well cooked). Macros are the same dry-pasta values used for the generic pasta entry.

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Quinoa (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.source: USDA FoodData Central (calculated from raw vs. cooked nutrient content ratios)

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Lentils (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Default is the boiled-or-baked preparation (289%), the more common one. Simmering for only 20 minutes leaves the lentils less hydrated (261%).

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Black Beans (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.source: USDA FoodData Central (calculated from raw vs. cooked nutrient content ratios - calorie and protein ratios agreed within 6 points)

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Chickpeas / Garbanzo Beans (dry)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Dry legume - expands rather than shrinks, similar to lentils and black beans
grains_pasta_legumes.source: USDA FoodData Central (calculated from raw vs. cooked nutrient content ratios - calorie and protein ratios agreed within 1.3 points)

grains_pasta_legumes.name: Soy Chunks (dry / textured vegetable protein)
grains_pasta_legumes.note: Dehydrated soy protein product, not a whole raw legume - absorbs a large amount of water when rehydrated/cooked. Popular high-protein staple in vegetarian diets, especially in India.
grains_pasta_legumes.source: IFCT 2017 (India's official Indian Food Composition Tables, calculated from raw vs. cooked nutrient content ratios - calorie and protein ratios agreed within 2 points). Not a USDA source, since USDA does not track this food, but IFCT is India's equivalent official nutrition authority.

vegetables.name: Broccoli
vegetables.note: Essentially no net weight change when boiled - water lost from the florets is offset by water taken up during cooking

vegetables.name: Spinach
vegetables.note: Spinach collapses dramatically in VOLUME but only loses about 23% of its WEIGHT when boiled - the common assumption of ~70% weight loss comes from watching the volume shrink, not from measurement. Steaming retains noticeably more weight than boiling (93% vs 77%), so how you cook it changes the result more than for most vegetables.

vegetables.name: Potato
vegetables.note: The 94% boiled figure is verified against USDA FoodData Central; the method breakdown is from USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 102 (1975). Baking with the skin oiled, and especially frying, drive off far more water than boiling.
vegetables.source: USDA FoodData Central (raw vs. cooked entries)

vegetables.name: Sweet Potato
vegetables.note: Baking drives off water (78%), while boiling and steaming hold it - boiled sweet potato even gains a little weight (101%).
